title: Best DORA Metrics Tools for Engineering Leaders in 2026
summary: Compare Weave, GitLab, Datadog, Apache DevLake and DX for delivery measurement. See why code output and review quality belong beside your DORA dashboard.
body_markdown:
## Overview


Weave combines deployment metrics with code-output analysis, review quality and AI costs. You can investigate whether faster releases accompanied more substantial work, smaller batches or more fixes, then open the changes behind the trend. This guide compares that engineering analysis with the delivery measurements in GitLab, Datadog, Apache DevLake and DX.


Weave reports **20–30% faster shipping** for customers using the platform.


GitLab is a natural starting point for teams already using its delivery records. Datadog puts deployment analysis beside service observability. Apache DevLake suits teams that want to operate and customize the measurement pipeline. DX combines system-based delivery reports with developer feedback and broader engineering analysis.


Weave publishes this comparison. The linked first-party definitions were reviewed November 13, 2026. Match each tool's event definitions to your service; the same “lead time” label can cover different intervals.


## What should a DORA metrics dashboard measure?


A release can contain a configuration fix or a major migration. Deployment frequency counts a release either way. That makes it useful for understanding delivery flow, while leaving the scope and outcome of the work for other measures.


Start with the current framework.[DORA’s official guide](https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics/) defines **five software delivery performance metrics** :


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Metric What to establish before comparing tools


Change lead time The time from a committed code change to its production deployment


Deployment frequency The production deployments counted within the reporting window


Failed deployment recovery time The time to recover from a deployment that needs immediate intervention


Change fail rate The share of deployments that require immediate intervention


Deployment rework rate The share of deployments that are unplanned responses to production incidents


Many products still document the earlier four-metric model. Some also retain the label “MTTR” or “time to restore service.” Ask which failures start the clock and which event stops it. A deployment failure, an incident, and an outage from another cause can produce different recovery measures.


Use DORA at the application or service level and follow the same service over time. Its[guidance on common pitfalls](https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics/#common-pitfalls) cautions against comparing unrelated applications or turning metric targets into competition.

The setup details matter more than a checkmark for “DORA supported.” For every candidate, ask whether deployment rework rate is available in the proposed configuration. The four-metric documentation linked here does not establish complete coverage of DORA’s current five-metric framework.


### Weave: inspect the work behind the delivery trend


[Weave Engineering Intelligence](https://weaveos.com/products/engineering-intelligence) combines deployment metrics with code output, reviews, reverts, churn and supported AI contribution signals.[Silk 1](https://weaveos.com/products/code-intelligence) reads code changes and estimates the work in a common unit of expert engineering effort. Its scores include reasoning and support team calibration.


This lets a leader investigate whether faster delivery accompanies a change in the work shipped. A higher release count could reflect smaller batches, more fixes, or a different project mix. Read code output and quality beside delivery to investigate work complexity and regressions.


Weave’s published delivery measures include deployment frequency, deployment success rate, deploy MTTR, and PR deploy lead time. Their definitions are worth checking closely:


- **PR deploy lead time starts at merge.** It is not the same interval as DORA’s commit-to-production lead time.
- **Deployment success rate describes deployment completion.** Its inverse is not automatically the share of releases that cause a production incident.
- **Deploy MTTR measures failed-deployment-to-next-successful-deployment time.** It should not be treated as incident resolution time without checking those events against the incident record.


Use those measures for the questions they answer. For procurement that requires every current DORA metric, validate the exact configuration and event evidence in the trial.


Follow a change through each stage. Weave's[PR cycle time](https://docs.weaveos.com/metrics/pr-cycle-time) runs from first commit to merge, while[PR merge time](https://docs.weaveos.com/metrics/pr-merge-time) starts when the PR opens.[Approval-to-merge time](https://docs.weaveos.com/metrics/pr-approval-to-merge-time) isolates the wait after approval, and[PR deploy lead time](https://docs.weaveos.com/metrics/pr-deploy-lead-time) starts at merge. These intervals locate different delays: work before opening, review and revision, waiting after approval, or the path into production. Keep the same interval and weekend setting when comparing teams or periods.


### GitLab


GitLab counts successful production deployments and measures lead time from merge. Failure and recovery measures depend on GitLab incidents. Its Duo and SDLC trends dashboard also includes supported AI activity, including documented Amazon Q support, with plan and data-store requirements.


#### What Weave adds over GitLab


Weave analyzes the code represented by the deployment. Its effort estimates distinguish a major refactor from a routine change, while review quality and turnover show the work required to get it ready. You can keep GitLab as the delivery source and add this analysis across connected repositories and AI tools.


That is useful when release frequency improves but leaders still need to understand output and cost. Weave's financial report can calculate a modeled return from engineering and AI costs; it does not turn merge-to-deploy time into hours saved.


[GitLab’s DORA documentation](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/analytics/dora_metrics/) ·[Duo and SDLC trends dashboard](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/analytics/duo_and_sdlc_trends/) ·[Weave](https://weaveos.com/products/code-intelligence) .


### Datadog


Datadog DORA Metrics uses deployments from APM or API/CLI, with Git metadata and configured failure detection. Results can be filtered by service, team, repository, environment and period.


#### What Weave adds over Datadog


Weave adds[code-effort analysis](https://weaveos.com/products/code-intelligence) and[review-quality assessment](https://docs.weaveos.com/metrics/review-quality) to the delivery trend. A service can deploy more often while its engineers spend more time revising the same area. Output, turnover, reverts and review rounds help investigate that pattern.


For AI-heavy teams, token and cost reporting adds the expense of producing those changes. Compare consumption with output and check the financial inputs before expanding a coding-tool rollout. Datadog's production observability still serves the separate task of tracing a deployment's effect on service health.


[Datadog DORA Metrics](https://docs.datadoghq.com/dora_metrics/) ·[setup guide](https://docs.datadoghq.com/dora_metrics/setup/) .


### Apache DevLake


Apache DevLake connects engineering records to Grafana dashboards, with configurable deployment and incident scope and inspectable SQL. It also collects AI-tool data, including Cursor usage and costs. The team operates the installation, ingestion and queries.


#### What Weave adds over Apache DevLake


Weave supplies an existing code-effort model, review assessment and financial ROI calculation instead of requiring your platform team to build those measures on top of collected events. Engineers can inspect and calibrate PR scores, and managers can save custom SQL or plain-English queries for the reports they need.


DevLake's self-hosted pipeline remains an option for organizations that want to own the calculations; Weave also offers enterprise on-premises deployment when location of processing is the requirement.


[Apache DevLake](https://devlake.apache.org/docs/DORA/) ·[Cursor plugin](https://github.com/apache/devlake/tree/main/backend/plugins/cursor) ·[release history](https://github.com/apache/devlake/releases) ·[Weave](https://weaveos.com/products/code-intelligence) .


### DX


DX supports self-reported snapshots and system-based DORA reporting. It distinguishes PR-open-to-deploy, merge-to-deploy and commit-to-deploy timing and offers complexity-weighted TrueThroughput.


#### What Weave adds over DX


Weave adds a defined expert-effort unit with PR explanations and team calibration. Use it beside deployment and review metrics to distinguish shorter delivery time from a change in the work being delivered.


AI Skills V2, developer surveys and review-quality analysis provide different follow-ups: coach verification, investigate reported friction or improve recurring review standards. DX also combines feedback and system data, so compare these specific assessments and workflows rather than treating developer feedback as unique to either product.


[DX documents two DORA setup paths](https://docs.getdx.com/reports/dora-metrics/) ·[TrueThroughput](https://getdx.com/truethroughput/) ·[Catalog analysis](https://docs.getdx.com/reports/catalog-analysis/) .


## Combine delivery, output and business measures


A useful engineering review can answer several questions without collapsing them into one score:


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Question Evidence to inspect


Are changes reaching production safely? Deployments, incidents, recovery, and rework


What engineering work shipped? Code changes, scope, output estimates, and review context


Is quality holding up? Reverts, defects, churn, review findings, and production behavior


Is AI investment helping? Adoption and cost alongside output, quality, and delivery over comparable periods


Did customers benefit? Product usage, reliability, customer feedback, and the relevant business outcome


Weave’s[Q2 2026 research report](https://weaveos.com/research/q2-2026) illustrates why activity and output should be examined separately: it analyzes PR volume alongside code-based output rather than treating them as interchangeable. The report's observational findings can help you choose which output and activity measures to follow. Compare your team's work over consistent periods and inspect the changes behind the results.


For AI budget decisions, the[AI ROI measurement guide](https://weaveos.com/blog/ai-roi-measurement-tools-for-engineering-teams) explains how spending, adoption, output, and quality fit together. Keep the service, team, time window, and cost basis consistent when comparing a change.


## Save delivery and code analysis in one report


Keep the delivery question ready for the next review. In a[custom dashboard](https://docs.weaveos.com/features/custom-dashboards) , managers with access can save delivery, code output, review quality and AI costs together. Add a[plain-English or SQL query](https://docs.weaveos.com/features/custom-queries) for the service or work category under discussion. Check its returned fields and records before comparing periods; missing production or incident events still need to come from the source system.


If releases are faster but AI spending is rising, open the code behind the output trend and check review burden and rework. Then compare[subscription costs with token-price estimates](https://docs.weaveos.com/metrics/ai-tool-costs) : more consumption on a flat-rate plan may not mean an equally larger invoice.


You can follow the same question from Claude or Cursor using Weave's[read-only MCP server](https://docs.weaveos.com/integrations/mcp) . Query the available engineering metrics and open the PR and review records your account can access. The deployment and recovery definitions above still apply.


## Investigate review before changing deployment targets


Some release delays begin before the deployment system receives the change. Weave measures review rounds and evaluates feedback for depth, communication, practicality and demonstrated impact. The[review-quality assessment](https://docs.weaveos.com/metrics/review-quality) can help distinguish careful, useful feedback from repeated corrections that could have been avoided. It does not infer defects a reviewer missed by scanning the entire PR.


Use[review turnaround](https://docs.weaveos.com/metrics/review-turnaround) to locate waiting, then[comment resolution](https://docs.weaveos.com/metrics/comment-resolution-rate) to see whether authors addressed feedback through a later commit or a clear reply. Review quality supplies the substance of the feedback. A fast deployment pipeline can coexist with long review waits or unresolved suggestions; the measures identify which part of the process needs attention before changing a deployment target.


## How to run a useful buying trial


Choose one production service and a reporting period that includes a normal release and a release requiring remediation. If no failed release exists in the sample, mark recovery and failure measures as untested. Do not interpret missing incidents as a zero failure rate.


1. **Agree on event definitions.** Record what counts as production, the lead-time start, the failure condition, the recovery event, and an unplanned remediation deployment.
2. **Reconcile the records.** Compare the tool with the release log and incident system. Account for staging runs, duplicate events, rollbacks, and changes spanning several services.
3. **Inspect a metric’s inputs.** Open a deployment, identify its commits or PRs, and follow a linked incident. Check missing-data behavior and aggregation rules.
4. **Investigate one constraint.** Decide whether the next action is reducing review delay, removing release friction, improving tests, or changing incident response. A dashboard should support that decision.
5. **Check ownership and cost.** Confirm the required plan, connectors, permissions, data retention, exports, and ongoing maintenance with each vendor. Compare the full operating cost rather than an unverified list price.


When evaluating Weave, include a feature, a fix, and a refactor in the code sample. Read the output explanations and ask engineers whether the scores reflect the work. Then inspect delivery and quality around those changes.

## Frequently asked questions


### What is the best DORA metrics tool?


Weave is our recommendation when the buying decision includes code output, review quality and AI investment as well as deployment health. GitLab, Datadog, DevLake and DX are useful alternatives for native delivery data, observability, self-hosted measurement and combined developer feedback respectively. Validate each required DORA definition against the same service.


### Can Git data alone produce a complete DORA dashboard?


Git history identifies code changes. Complete delivery measurement also needs reliable production deployment and failure evidence. A merge is not proof that code reached users. Confirm how each tool obtains the missing events and labels any inferred data.


### Are DORA metrics and engineering output the same thing?


They answer different questions. DORA describes delivery performance. Code output analysis examines the work inside changes. Customer and business outcomes need their own evidence. Use them together when evaluating an engineering investment.


### Does a four-metric dashboard cover the current framework?


Not necessarily. DORA’s current guide includes deployment rework rate as a fifth metric. Ask for the definition, event source, and a worked example for each required measure, including recovery metrics with older names.
